cards.title: Scroll-stopping hook mechanisms and when each works
cards.summary: Nine hook archetypes for paid and organic creative, with the awareness stage each one resonates with.
cards.use_when: Writing the first 3 seconds of acquisition creative (Meta/TikTok/YouTube) or organic content, and deciding which hook angle to test for a given audience.
steps: Problem call-out ('struggling with back pain from desk work?'): only resonates with problem-aware audiences — good performance but not scalable above that awareness stage, so pair it with audience-specific targeting rather than scaling it broadly.

Contrarian truth: challenge a common assumption ('everything you've been told about protein timing is wrong'). Creates cognitive friction that demands resolution; the source says this works across all awareness levels and in organic and paid.
Specific proof: lead with a measurable outcome including numbers and time frames ('lost 12kg in 90 days without giving up pasta') to build credibility inside the hook.
Curiosity gap: create an information gap only closed by watching. The source reports average view time over 45 seconds on one such hook in their own organic content.

Price/ingredient/industry truth bomb: lead with the uncomfortable truth ('this product costs $120, it's expensive, but it's our best seller — here's why'). The source says this works best for premium or high-AOV products where price is the main objection, cutting through on cold audiences, but is only relevant to specific industries.

Psychological confrontation: direct, interruptive statements that feel like a friend calling you out ('that drawer full of products you never use — that's the problem'). Plays on emotional pain and makes the viewer feel personally addressed as a scroll stopper.

Texture/ASMR hook: 2–3 seconds of close-up fabric handling, squeezing, pouring, or unboxing with no words. The source says this does very well in fashion and is a current high performer in their accounts.

Founder's letter: open with origin story plus real, unfakeable risk ('I remortgaged my house and put $300,000 down for the first order'). The source says the more genuine risk in the hook, the better — but it must be a real circumstance.
Social proof: lead with a credibility marker ('90% of customers saw results in 30 days').

You can likely apply at least seven of these to your brand now. Ask an LLM for more hook types, then translate them to your brand — but the source stresses scripting (not just the hook list) is what makes ads stand out.
caveats: Problem call-outs cap scalability at that awareness stage per the source.
The $120 price hook and ASMR/texture hook are industry-specific per the source.
Founder risk hooks only work when the risk is real; faking it undermines the effect.

cards.title: Bridge scripting: never jump from hook to product
cards.summary: The hook-to-body and body-to-CTA bridges are where most ads break; introduce the product gradually instead of abruptly.
cards.use_when: Scripting or editing video ads (and writing paid social copy) where the product appears mid-creative and you need to keep viewers from feeling suddenly sold to.
steps: Identify your two bridges: hook→body and body→CTA. The source says these are frequently done badly even when hook, body, and CTA scripting are individually strong.

Avoid the abrupt version: 'are you training for a marathon and want better recovery? Well, creatine from [brand] is your solution.' The source says this ad won't do well — hook, body, and CTA can all be good and the bridge still ruins the whole asset.

Think of the ad as a curve: y-axis = product awareness, x-axis = time. A huge step change in product awareness mid-asset makes viewers go from 'I'm being taught something' to 'I'm being sold to', which people dislike.
Blend the product introduction in gradually so awareness rises smoothly. The source treats this as largely intuitive: introduce the product, don't suddenly drop it in.

In top-of-funnel unaware ads, move viewers through awareness stages across the ad: unaware → problem aware → solution aware → product aware → conversion (often on a retargeting ad). Example progression from the source: unaware hook → 'tap water doesn't have electrolytes and is bad for me' (problem) → 'you need this amount of salt in this ratio' (solution) → 'there's a canned mineral water with electrolytes' (product).
Do NOT introduce the product by the 90-second mark just because the retention curve drops 80% by then. The source calls this the wrong way to think.

Introduce the product as late as possible so viewers are pre-framed, high-intent and ready to buy. The source says later product introduction and CTA often yields better conversion rates and higher total purchase volume, even with fewer total viewers.
caveats: The 'introduce as late as possible' rule is the source's argument against retention-curve-driven scripting; it is a stated trade-off (fewer total people, higher intent) rather than a universal law.
VSSL-style video sales letters execute this staging well per the source, but require strong scriptwriting skill.

cards.title: Hook testing still works post-Andromeda — and it's cheap
cards.summary: Changing only the first 3 seconds produces a distinct Meta creative ID that gets its own audience and can resurrect fatigued winners.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep investing in hook variations versus building entirely new concepts, especially when a proven ad has fatigued.
steps: Confirm the mechanics: Meta will recognize a different hook as a different creative, assign it its own creative ID, and it won't be pulled together with the original asset — it will reach a novel unique audience.
Accept that some overlap remains: the remaining ~87 seconds talk to the same person with the same problem and the same offer, so in the concept framework it's still the same concept.
Do it anyway because it's nearly free: record 6 hooks while shooting the ad (a few extra minutes) to get 6 variations, or attach new hooks to existing high performers.
Use it to revive winners: the source reports ads that spent $50k–$100k and fatigued, then spent another ~$100k at the same efficiency after rotating in ~50 new hooks that took about an hour to shoot.
Use it to rescue failures: ads that didn't work with a bad hook rate can be made to work by fixing the hook.
The source treats hook testing as still the highest-leverage point in videos, organic ads, and YouTube content.
caveats: Spend-resurrection figures are the source's own case examples, not benchmarks.
Assumes the body, offer, and audience remain valid — only the hook is the variable.

cards.title: Five questions to choose the right ad format
cards.summary: Define concept first, then decide format by education need, single-frame communicability, product demo need, and awareness stage.
cards.use_when: Planning a creative production batch for a product or persona — deciding video vs static vs carousel before briefing production.
steps: Start with the concept, not the format. Build persona → angle → offer first, then choose the format. The source calls format the last step; you don't start with format and work backwards.
Ask: does this concept require education? If yes, lean toward a longer-form asset (typically video) that can educate.

Ask: can the value prop be communicated in a single frame? If yes, lean toward images and carousels, which are cheap and quick to produce in volume. Whenever you can produce statics over video, the source generally advises doing so.
Ask: does the product need a demo? This constrains how much you can do with images unless you have a strong designer.
Ask: what stage of awareness are we in? Low awareness (product aware / aware) can use DPAs and images with bottom-of-funnel ads; high awareness needs longer education-format video.

Two approaches to statics: (a) use statics to fast-test angles and concepts, then develop winners into deeper video assets; (b) double down on statics where cheap production outweighs better-but-expensive video performance.
The source stresses that 'statics are bottom-of-funnel' and 'video is top-of-funnel' is a skill issue — top-of-funnel statics are possible if designed that way.
caveats: Awareness-stage format mapping is the source's heuristic, not a measured rule.
The claim that anyone doing under hundreds of thousands of dollars per day on images has a 'skill issue' is the presenter's opinion, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Cost of production versus contribution margin per ad — the image vs video decision
cards.summary: Calculate average contribution margin per ad against cost of producing it, split by format, to decide where to double down.
cards.use_when: Allocating creative production budget between images and video, or diagnosing why an ad account isn't scaling despite decent ad performance.
steps: Compute average revenue per ad unit. The source reports that for most accounts this is around $2,000ish.
Delineate revenue down to contribution margin per ad unit: subtract gross profit and the cost of serving the ad. Example from source: ~$350 contribution margin per ad unit.
Compare to cost of producing a single ad. In the source's example, $400 per ad — the equation doesn't work because you're paying more to produce than you make in contribution margin.

Break the calculation down by format: images might cost ~$50 and return ~$300; videos might cost ~$500 and return ~$400. Even if video performs better per ad, the cost-of-production-to-contribution-margin ratio can favor images.

If the ratio favors images, double down on images. The source cites people doing $200,000/day in revenue on AI images and says there's no reason you can't do hundreds of thousands per day on images only.
Use this calculation as an account-level diagnostic, not just a format choice: the source runs it for clients during onboarding specifically to understand average revenue per ad in the account.
caveats: The $2,000 / $350 / $400 / $50 / $300 / $500 figures are illustrative examples from the source, not benchmarks you should assume apply.
These are the source's calculations; you must use your own numbers and your own gross profit and serving costs.

cards.title: Advertorial statics: make the ad look like an organic post
cards.summary: Advertorial static ads work by mimicking platform-native content formats and only revealing the sale in the copy, paired with an educational landing experience.
cards.use_when: Designing top-of-funnel static creative for cold audiences, especially in health/wellness or older demographics.
steps: Use a native format: repost a tweet-style post that feels organic to the platform rather than a branded ad unit.

Reinforce the organic feel by running through a creator or expert profile (whitelisting) rather than a partnership ad with both brand and creator handles visible. The source notes IM8 ran it through Dr. James' profile without a brand collaboration, so you don't know it's an ad until you read the copy underneath.

Widen the problem to maximize total addressable market: list a broad set of symptoms (dry eyes, poor vision, low energy, bad skin, cracks at the mouth, fatigue, bleeding gums, painful muscles, excessive bruising) and attribute them to the deficiency category your product addresses.

Educate inside the creative: identify the deficiency and what resolves it, then introduce the product ('the best multivitamin equals [brand] daily ultimate 10% off'), with more education on how the product works.
Keep the CTA at the bottom so it is clickable directly from the post.

The source says advertorial statics only perform well if the click leads to an education-based landing page or the primary text itself educates heavily — otherwise the native feel sets up the wrong expectation.
caveats: The source reports the IM8 tweet static performed very well (47,000 likes) — a single example, not a promise.
Running through a creator's handle changes the target audience: the source says it likely reaches that creator's audience, which is desirable only if the creator is contextually relevant.

cards.title: Review/round-up advertorial funnel with a dermatologist framing
cards.summary: A 'best products of the year' review article run through a doctor's page, ranking competitors badly and the brand best, feeding a quiz funnel.
cards.use_when: Building a top-of-funnel static ad plus education page for a product with many alternatives and authority-driven demand (hair growth, supplements, skincare).
steps: Write the ad as a ranking article headline: 'The best hair growth products of 2025 and the ones to avoid — what the big brands aren't telling you.' Assume the reader thinks they're going to get an unbiased blog article.

Run it through an authoritative profile (in the source example a dermatologist page) with short copy establishing mission and authority ('as a dermatologist, I set out on a mission to find the most effective hair growth products'), then a 'learn more' link.
Land on a review-style page owned by the brand. Establish who the person is and their authority, then rank all products, giving extensive reasons why each is or isn't recommended.
Make only your product clickable in the ranking list (competitors are not clickable), and route the click into a custom landing page and quiz funnel that pushes to conversion.
Handle the people who don't click your product: the source's example routes secondary rankings to an Amazon affiliate link, retaining some value from non-converters.
Maintain light compliance framing using comparison criteria and green/red ticks so the review format reads as a comparison rather than a pure ad.
caveats: The source's assessment of effectiveness ('I imagine this is doing quite well for them') is speculative, not a measured result.
The format is ethically sensitive: it presents a brand-owned page as an independent review. The source openly points out the 'giveaway' (only one product is clickable).
Compliance considerations vary by market and category.

cards.title: Long-form copy statics for 50+ demographics
cards.summary: Static image ads with very long copy that pull an unaware audience through all awareness stages perform strongly on Facebook feeds for 50+ audiences.
cards.use_when: Building cold-audience creative for an older target demographic where long copy and story-based education can convert.
steps: Serve static image ads with long-form copy on Facebook feeds when the target demographic is 50+ — the source says this ad type 'crushes' there.
Write a long story that starts at an unaware audience and pulls them through: unaware → problem aware → solution aware → product aware → able to convert.
Treat this as a copywriting skill problem, not a format problem: the source says you can be AI assisted, but without fundamentals of emotionally appealing to a specific demographic, it won't work.

For the same demographic, the source says VSSL-style video sales letters also do very well because they walk through all awareness stages and are highly educational. AI-generated VSSLs can work end-to-end, and the source reports some hold hundreds of thousands in ad spend.
caveats: The source states these ads 'crush on cold audiences' but flags they require enormous copywriting skill.
AI VSSL performance is described as variable: 'some do quite well, some unbelievably well' — not a guaranteed outcome.

cards.title: VSSL script structure: persona call-out, objection handling, problem agitation, then late product reveal
cards.summary: How to run a video sales letter that educates and handles objections before introducing the product.
cards.use_when: Scripting a video sales letter or long-form educational ad for a problem/solution category like supplements or health.
steps: Open with a persona call-out that filters viewers: 'you have IBS, leaky gut, or bloating? You're probably missing this one thing.'
Move to objection handling immediately: name the conventional fix ('your doctor probably told you to manage it with a course of pills') and reframe it as treating the symptom, not the cause.

Problem agitate and open a curiosity gap: 'here's what they're not telling you', plus an educational mechanism explanation (e.g. the gut as an ecosystem, bacteria imbalance, inflammation, nutrient absorption).

Increase the total addressable market when you prescribe a problem, because the immediate viewer reaction to a disease or physical issue is denial ('I probably have it' or 'it's probably rare'). Stating '40% of people have this, most don't know, you might be among them' keeps people watching.
Handle objections around competitor alternatives (e.g. throwing probiotics at the problem is like sending a single soldier into a war zone) before introducing your product.
Introduce the product, then explain the mechanism step by step (enzymes, prebiotics, 10 billion CFU probiotics, postbiotics) and give social proof (e.g. '85% in a 12-week clinical trial').

The source flags two AI-scripting tells to avoid where possible: 'contrast negation' ('it's not X, it's Y' — 'your gut isn't broken, it's starving') and the 'complete military operation, not a single soldier' style metaphor.
The source's improvement note: extend the bridge by ~15 seconds to educate on why the ingredients fix the issue before introducing the brand as the solution holding those ingredients.
caveats: The source's example ad has 25 million views and has run 3–4 years — a single exceptional case, not a benchmark.
The source treats contrast negation as something they avoid rather than a proven failure mode.
VSSLs require sustained educational value; the source says some AI VSSLs do well and some unbelievably well, implying wide variance.

cards.title: Objection-handling UGC spliced onto the front of a VSSL
cards.summary: A proven VSSL format with contrarian takes and split-screen engagement, plus objection-handling UGC at the front.
cards.use_when: Producing long-form video ads for cold audiences where you want to keep people watching via contrarian framing before an educational body.
steps: Open with a split-screen UGC/news-style framing to add engagement and context, as in the source's example where a presenter reviews a celebrity trainer's claims.

Stack contrarian takes repeatedly through the opening (~first 28 seconds in the source example): celebrate the contrarian, then validate the person after the fact ('turns out he's a celebrity trainer who's gained a massive following for challenging mainstream advice').
Use the stack of contrarian takes to string viewers along while hinting at your own system, creating a broad curiosity gap: 'if no one needs to cut carbs, what is the actual solution?'
Move into the educational body and eventually sell your system (body types, programming, etc.) after creating the gap.

Alternative structure from a second example: open with contrarian hook, then alternate problem agitation and education ('problem agitate, then educate' repeatedly) using a faceless format better suited to education and organic feel.

Handle objections around the core premise of the hook — e.g. after naming TRT, explain the side effects (hair loss, high estrogen, gyno, mood swings, infertility, acne, injections) before introducing the natural alternative.
Introduce the product late — the source notes the Natty Plus product appears about a minute and a half in, which is cited as the reason the ad scales.
Keep it fast-cut, constantly changing formats, and native to the platform; run it on an influencer profile so viewers think it's educational content rather than an ad.
caveats: The source's example ads are high performers on specific influencer profiles with existing audiences; results depend on the creator/brand fit.
The source explicitly notes the product-late structure is why it works, but this is presented as their interpretation of the ad, not tested proof.

cards.title: Incremental attribution: read DPA ROAS correctly before scaling bottom of funnel
cards.summary: DPAs show inflated attributed ROAS because they credit existing customers and non-incremental conversions; use incremental attribution to see the real number.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget to put into DPA/carousel retargeting, particularly in fashion, and evaluating whether bottom-of-funnel is scalable on cold audiences.
steps: Understand what a DPA is: a carousel ad that dynamically pulls in products the user visited on your site, provided your pixel is passing back page-view data.
Remove existing customers from the ROAS view first. The source says when you delineate out existing customers, the DPA ROAS drops precipitously.
Then delineate to incremental attribution: in Meta, click Columns → Compare Attribution Settings → Incremental Attribution → Apply. You then get a split of the incremental ROAS for the ad.

Understand the calculation conceptually: Meta holds out roughly 10% of the targeted audience daily. If 1% of the holdout converts and 2% of the exposed group converts, the difference-in-difference is 1% — so the ad's real impact is 1%, not 2%. In the source's example, a 5 attributed ROAS should be adjusted down ~50% to ~2.5.
Treat DPA ROAS as lower than it appears, particularly on new audiences. The source says they have yet to see an ad account where DPA is a great scalable ad type on cold audiences.
The source's limits on DPA scale: it can work on cold audiences and can absorb ~$1,000/day in some accounts, but it cannot be scaled to $50,000/day on cold.

Watch for the death spiral: because DPAs sit at the bottom of the funnel with good-looking attributed ROAS, brands pull budget out of top of funnel and into DPAs, which shrinks the top-of-funnel user quantity, scales something non-scalable, and topples the whole funnel with declining ROAS.
caveats: The 5.0→2.5 conversion is an illustrative example, not a fixed correction factor.
Specific Meta interface steps must be verified in the current Ads Manager, as the interface may change.
Incrementality methodology via holdouts is Meta's, and the source's description is simplified.

cards.title: Funnel and creative-production budget split: 70–90% top, 20% middle, 5–10% bottom
cards.summary: Because campaign structure no longer enforces funnel splits, allocate by creative production volume — most assets at high awareness stages.
cards.use_when: Planning how many top, middle, and bottom of funnel creative assets to produce in the next cycle, and where to focus budget.
steps: Target a rough split: 70–90% of budget to top of funnel, ~20% to middle of funnel, and 5–10% to bottom of funnel.

Recognize why you can't enforce this through campaign structure anymore: the source says there's a lack of campaign structure now, and you should consolidate rather than building separate top/middle/bottom campaigns (except keeping bottom of funnel separate).
Therefore allocate by creative production volume: 70–90% of the assets you make should be at high awareness stages, ~20% at middle-to-bottom stages.
Protect top of funnel: the failure mode is pulling budget from 'bad ROAS' top-of-funnel efforts into bottom-of-funnel DPAs, which shrinks the top-of-funnel user pool and topples the funnel.
The source notes a more precise way to calculate bottom-of-funnel budgeting appears later in their video, and that this split is a rough guide.
caveats: The split is a rough heuristic from the source, not a calculated target for every business.
Campaign structure flexibility is intentional: the source says account structure should match the complexity of the business, not follow one template.

cards.title: Partnership ads: using creator audience data for cold targeting
cards.summary: Ads run through the creator's handle use both handles' audience data to find new cold users and feel more authentic.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to invest in creator collaborations or whitelisting/partnership ads and how heavily to weight them in the account.
steps: Set up the ad so it runs through the creator's profile: your brand name can appear alongside the influencer's handle, and the source notes a setting lets Meta change combinations and split test to find the best mix (sometimes brand, sometimes creator, sometimes both).

Understand why they perform: targeting uses the audience on both handles, so if the creator is contextually relevant to your target demographic, the ad reaches their audience and uses their audience data to find new people — effectively leveraging the creator's audience for cold targeting, not just warm.
They also feel more authentic: receiving an ad from an influencer profile feels less like being sold to, and organic-feeling content resonates better.

The source reports running up to 40% of total account spend through partnership or collaborator ads in some accounts they work on, and says brands not running them are at a disadvantage versus competitors.
The source flags this as an arbitrage that may be closing — if you're watching much later, the opportunity may already be gone.
caveats: The 40% of spend figure is from the source's own accounts, not a universal target.
Contextually relevant creators are required for the audience-leveraging benefit; source says they hope the creator is relevant.
The source explicitly warns the arbitrage may end.

cards.title: Testing cycle: hypothesis, volume, launch, analyze, scale, iterate
cards.summary: How to run a creative testing cycle given a typical hit rate, including how many ads to make per concept.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new creative test for a concept, or deciding how many ads are needed before judging whether a concept works.
steps: Build a hypothesis: define what you're actually testing. Typically the test is the concept, specifically one of the four variables you're changing in the concept.

Build a batch of ads under that concept — at least 10+. The source's reasoning: most accounts have around a 5% hit rate, so technically you'd need at least 20 ads to expect a winner if your hit rate is 5%.
Think about your account's hit rate as the function that determines how much volume you need to validate a hypothesis.

Launch into your testing structure, then analyze against the hypothesis: what did you expect, how much spend did you want to go through, how many conversions did you expect, what was the ROI — and how did actual compare?
If it worked, look at strategies to scale. If not, iterate. The source notes iteration gets faster as ad spend grows.
caveats: The ~5% hit rate and 20-ads-to-expect-a-winner are the source's account averages, not universal; your own hit rate changes the required volume.
The source stresses account structure flexibility: complexity of the account should be a product of the complexity of the business.

cards.title: When to add ads to an adset vs launch a new adset
cards.summary: Don't disrupt a winning adset's learning phase; if it's below KPI, change anything you want.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add new creative to an existing adset or create a new adset, based on whether the adset is hitting KPI.
steps: Set a floor of a minimum of 3 ads per adset, with a maximum of probably 50–100 based on budget; the source says to think about the lower limit, not the upper.

If the adset is hitting KPI and scaling well, do NOT add new ads to it. Adding ads resets the learning phase to some degree because sequencing across creatives is disrupted and the system relearns how to distribute spend. The source says they've personally wrecked performance this way.
If the adset is not hitting KPI and is underperforming, do whatever you want: turn ads off, add as many as you want. You'll break some sequencing, but the sequencing isn't working anyway.

If a concept is working and you make more ads for it (e.g. 20 more), launch them in a NEW adset named to indicate it's the same concept (e.g. 'concept one, shoot two'), so you can filter them together.

For scaling, increase budgets — never turn off a winning ad and relaunch it in a scaling campaign, which the source calls a rookie mistake. You can copy post IDs into a scaling campaign as an option; it works in some accounts and not others.

Typical structure the source recommends for small to mid-size businesses: a testing campaign with concepts at adset level, optionally a separate bottom-of-funnel retargeting campaign that lets you exclude existing customers from the testing campaign so it stays cold, and optionally a mid-funnel adset on 90-day website visitors if you need to increase frequency on engaged audiences.
caveats: The source says this structure suits small to mid-size businesses and will evolve as the business evolves; it is not meant for a very large multi-SKU retailer.
Whether to use ABO or CBO is described as personal preference in the source, with risk trade-offs explained separately.
The 90-day mid-funnel adset only makes sense if you believe you need more frequency on engaged audiences.

cards.title: Metrics ranked by reliability for judging creative
cards.summary: Amount spent is the best proxy for creative performance, followed by 7-day click or incremental ROAS/CPA, then CPC/CTR, with hook and hold rates as diagnostics only.
cards.use_when: Reviewing creative performance in the ad account to decide which ads to scale, cut, or iterate on.
steps: Rank the metrics: (1) amount spent, (2) ROAS or CPA using 7-day click or incremental attribution, (3) CPC and CTR, (4) hook rate and hold rate (video only).

Treat amount spent as the top proxy for extended-period performance. Because attribution only goes to the last ad, an ad that gets all the budget despite a lower reported ROAS is probably causing purchases elsewhere in the account — e.g. a 1.7 ROAS creative with double the spend of a 2.2 creative is likely the better top-of-funnel asset with low frequency cutting through new audiences.

Use CPC and CTR as leading indicators, particularly on the fringes: if your account average CPC is around a certain level and no ad above that level has ever been profitable, it's a signal those ads will never work because traffic is too expensive. The source gives the example of a ~$3 CPC threshold.

Use hook rate (how many people make it past 3 seconds) and hold rate (source's general definition: past 15 seconds) as diagnostic tools only — they are not correlated with conversion performance. Use them to iterate: a terrible hook rate against your average means switch the hook; a bad hold rate means people didn't hold through the bridge, so fix the bridge and redo that part.
In practice, combine multiple metrics in conjunction to assess creative quality rather than relying on any single one.
caveats: Only use 7-day click or incremental attribution views; standard attribution misstates performance.
Hook and hold rate definitions vary; the source uses multiple definitions in their own reporting.
The ~$3 CPC example is illustrative, not a benchmark to adopt.

cards.title: ABO vs CBO: risk tolerance trade-off via Pareto's principle
cards.summary: CBO concentrates spend into a tiny share of ads, improving efficiency but raising fatigue and portfolio risk; ABO de-risks but typically at slightly lower ROI.
cards.use_when: Choosing campaign budgeting method for a product portfolio, or deciding when to switch to CBO to spike efficiency.
steps: Understand the mechanics: with CBO, the campaign distributes budget however it wants, and Pareto's principle applies — 20% of ads drive 80% of revenue. The source says Pareto compounds: within that 80%, 80% is driven by 20%, so roughly 4% of ads hold about 64% of total spend and revenue generation.
Accepting CBO means accepting that most of your budget goes to ~4% of ads — best efficiency and performance, but very high risk because if those ads fatigue you have no backups.

Recognize the portfolio management cost: CBO is described as terrible for portfolio management because you over-lever into a few ads, and at product level 20% of products drive 80% of revenue, so spend skews to a few SKUs and sell-through rates across your portfolio become harder to control.
Frame the choice as a trade-off: CBO = increased risk, likely increased ROI; lower-risk approach = slightly lower ROI.
Use CBO selectively for a quick spike in efficiency when ROI is below where you need it and de-risking/testing isn't the current priority. The source says they would switch to CBO in those periods.
Aim for a steady state of de-risked spend across more ads and more products, so that if something stops working you aren't in a terrible position.
The source says they personally, if running the business, would choose the lower-risk approach in most cases depending on season and business stage.
caveats: The 4%/64% figure is the source's own ad account analysis, not a universal constant.
The CBO risk/ROI trade-off is presented as a preference and situational choice, not a universal rule.
Product-level concentration under CBO depends on portfolio size and whether multiple products sit under one CBO.

cards.title: Fix the 90/10 desire vs pain-point creative imbalance
cards.summary: Many large retailers skew creative toward campaign-shoot desire imagery and under-invest in pain-point-led performance assets.
cards.use_when: Auditing existing creative mix, especially for a retailer with a legacy campaign shoot process, and rebalancing production budgets toward performance assets.
steps: Audit your current creative mix through the lens of desire vs pain-point-led content. The source describes a '90/10 problem' in many large retailers they audit (including nine-figure Australian retailers) where desire-led creative dominates.

Diagnose the cause: many large retailers were built around campaign shoots. Campaign shoots do one thing — build desire — with models and shots that make people want the product, but they don't play to pain points at all.
Shift the ratio toward pain: the source says the best performance marketing assets sit on pain and recommends moving toward 60/40 pain/desire, with the best brands probably closer to 70/30.
Use the framing of performance-marketing-driven assets vs branding-driven assets to categorize your existing library and decide what to produce next.
The source says to look at whether you actually have any pain-led creative at all — a 90/10 split implies nearly all creative is desire-led.
caveats: The 60/40 and 70/30 ratios are the source's recommendations, not measured results.
The 90/10 problem is presented as observed across the source's client base, not a universal retailer statistic.
Some categories may reasonably need more desire-led branding creative.

cards.title: Bottom-of-funnel retargeting as objection handling
cards.summary: Model why the 95% of site visitors who didn't buy didn't buy, and build retargeting creative to answer each objection type.
cards.use_when: Building bottom-of-funnel retargeting for a product or category, and diagnosing why retargeting creative is underperforming.
steps: Start from the math: a 5% website conversion rate means 95% of visitors did not buy. Ask why — what were their objections?
Segment the objections approximately (the source's illustrative split): price, trust in the brand, quality concerns, and not-ready-yet / too soon.

Answer the price objection with discounts, value anchoring, and cost-per-use angles. The source says cost-per-use creatives 'crush' on bottom of funnel — e.g. for a supplement, compare it to the price of a coffee.
Answer the trust objection with social proof: how many customers you have, how many five-star reviews you have, and user-generated content testimonials.
